title: Should we break up before the holidays or wait until after?
summary: Break up before the holidays or wait until after? An honest look at what each choice costs, and how to tell real waiting from avoiding.
body_markdown:
There is no kind week on the calendar for this. If you are looking for the date where ending a relationship won't land on anybody, you will not find it, and the looking is usually how people end up asking this same question again next November.


So, straight answer: the holidays are not a reason to leave, and they are not a reason to stay. They are a deadline you did not choose, pressing on a decision you have mostly already made. The question actually worth answering is whether waiting is something you are choosing, or something that is quietly choosing for you.


## Two very different reasons to wait


Waiting can be a real decision. Your partner's mother is sick and this is probably her last Christmas. The flights are booked and nonrefundable. Your kid is seven, and you do not want December to be the month they think of for the rest of their life. Those are reasons. Carrying a few more weeks so that someone you still care about is not gutted on a specific date is not cowardice. It is a choice with a cost you have agreed to pay.


Waiting can also be a place to set the decision down. "After the holidays" is one of the most comfortable deadlines in the language, because it never quite arrives. It becomes[after New Year's](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-this-be-the-year-i-leave) . Then after their birthday. Then not now, they just started the new job. A year goes by and you are still *about to* .


There is a quick way to tell the two apart. Say the date out loud, to yourself, with an actual number in it. January the sixth. If a real date makes your stomach drop, you are planning something. If you can only say "after the holidays," and saying it brings relief rather than dread, the vagueness is doing a job for you, and the job is not kindness.


## What each choice actually costs


Both options cost something. It helps to know which bill you are signing rather than hunting for the one that is free.


Ending it now means the season carries it. There will be a Christmas in their memory that was the one. Their family will likely be nearby, which can mean support for them, and can also mean an audience.[You will spend some of the season alone](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/i-want-to-leave-but-im-scared) , or explaining. And you will do the telling while everyone around you is in a good mood.


[Waiting means several weeks of performing](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/pretending-everything-is-fine-in-front-of-family) . Buying a gift when you already know. Someone's aunt asking when you two are finally going to make it official. A shared bed in a guest room. The[particular loneliness of sitting at a full table](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/lonely-in-my-relationship-during-the-holidays) next to a person you have privately already left. That last one is heavier than people expect, and it is the piece most likely to come out sideways in the car on the way home, usually disguised as[an argument about whose family you are seeing](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/fighting-about-whose-family-for-the-holidays) .


## What comes up in Maia conversations around this time of year


When people bring this decision to Maia, they almost always open with the other person's Christmas. A few layers in, it is frequently about being seen. What they are dreading is not the conversation itself. It is telling their mother. It is the photograph in their head of the kind of person who does this in December.


The other thing we hear a lot: someone says they are waiting so they do not ruin the holidays, and then describes a holiday they are already not really present for. The relationship ended months ago in every way except the announcement. In that situation, waiting does not protect the season. It just means everyone spends it with a version of you who is not there.


None of which means go now. It means being precise about what you are actually protecting, and for whom.


## If you decide to wait, decide what you are waiting with


Waiting on purpose is a legitimate choice. It works much better with some edges on it.


- **Give it a date and write it down.** Somewhere you will see it. A deadline you can move in your head is not a deadline.
- **Do not make new promises.** Skip the grand gift. Do not agree to the trip in March or the lease renewal, and do not let "next year we should" go unanswered in front of their family. Small, honest, no forward motion.
- **Do not use the season as evidence.** Three tender days in December do not undo the last eight months, and a bad fight on the twenty-third is not proof either. The holidays make everyone a slightly exaggerated version of themselves.
- **Tell one person.** Not the family, not yet. One friend who can know what you are carrying. Doing this in total silence for six weeks is what makes it feel unsurvivable.
- **Notice if you are actually unsure.** Some people find, once they name the date, that the dread is not about timing at all. If the real question is[whether this is fixable or finished](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) , that is a different question and it deserves its own attention, not a January deadline.


Some people try to split the difference and propose[a break until January](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/is-taking-a-break-the-fast-track-to-breaking-up) . That can be a genuine reset for some couples. Going into the holidays specifically, it more often works as a softer version of the same vagueness, with the added cost that the other person now spends the whole season waiting for a verdict.


## The version of waiting that costs the most


Half-leaving. Staying in the house but going cold. Answering in one word, disappearing into your phone, being technically present and completely gone.


Your partner will feel it. They just will not have language for it, so they will chase you, or pick fights, or get anxious in a way that later gets filed as more evidence that you were right to go. That is the version that leaves lasting damage, and it is not about timing. It is about weeks of being told nothing is wrong while everything is.


If you are going to wait, wait warmly. Otherwise do not wait.


If you are still turning this over, that is not weakness or indecision. It is a real question with a real price either way. Talking it through with Maia can help you work out whether you are choosing to wait or hiding inside the waiting, and what you want the next several weeks to actually look like. There is no preferred answer here. The point is only that you know which one you picked, and why.
